detail: The killing blow on the boss reported the wrong reason for the phase ending. fe7_act(#4 Wil, 9, 10, action:'attack', target_slot:0) killed Heintz and returned: "Self: HP 24/24, and it was the last unspent unit, so the player phase ended." That claim is false — SIX units were still unspent at that moment (#0 Lyn at (13,7), #3 Florina at (10,11), #5 Dorcas at (12,9), #6 at (13,5), #7 at (13,3), #10 Nils at (13,6), #11 at (13,4)). The phase ended because the CHAPTER ended: fe7_unstick immediately afterwards read phase 0x40, turn 0, text buffer "Ch. 7x: The Black Shadow". The tool appears to infer "last unspent unit" from the has-acted flags being cleared plus the phase byte moving, which is exactly what a chapter transition also looks like — the same ambiguity fe7_act's own 'wait' documentation warns about, resolved the wrong way here. This is the dangerous failure shape: had I believed it, I would have gone looking for why six units silently lost their turn. Note also that Wil's max HP is printed as 24/24 in this line but 23/23 everywhere before it — he levelled up on the kill, which is fine, but it means the line mixes a pre- and post-level-up reading without saying so.
wanted: Check for chapter completion BEFORE attributing the phase change to the unit, and say which happened: "CHAPTER COMPLETE — objective met (phase 0x40, turn reset to 0, next chapter 'Ch. 7x: The Black Shadow')" instead of "it was the last unspent unit". The turn counter resetting to 0 and the phase going to 0x40 rather than 0x80 already distinguish the two cases without needing the game-over flag located. More generally there is no tool that answers "is the chapter over and did I win" — fe7_wait can only prove two LOSS conditions and infers them; a chapter-complete signal is the missing other half, and it is cheap here because the turn counter reset is unambiguous.

detail: The whole run's shape was set by one thing the tools do not do: fe7_act commits a unit's turn in a single call, so ordering a nine-unit march through a one-tile funnel means nine sequential calls per turn, each of which I have to pre-compute destinations for BY HAND against a cost grid I can only see for one unit at a time. Concrete instances this run: (a) I repeatedly issued a move that was refused because an ally I had not moved yet was standing on the destination — fe7_act(#4 Wil, 3, 5) was refused with "OCCUPIED by a ally unit (slot #11)", and I had to reorder; (b) crossing the (13,5)-(13,6) mountain funnel took turns 6, 7 and 8 to file eight units through, and I hand-computed each unit's stopping tile from the previous unit's vacated tile; (c) fe7_reachable's grid is only valid until anyone moves, so after every single fe7_act every other unit's grid is stale and I plan the rest of the turn from memory. It worked — the chapter is won on turn 9 with no deaths — but the reason job 1 went fine is that I spent most of my thinking on tile arithmetic rather than on tactics.
wanted: A whole-turn planner rather than a whole-unit one. fe7_plan({moves:[{slot,x,y,action,target_slot},...]}) that (1) validates ALL destinations against the cost maps simulating the moves in sequence, so a conflict is reported before anything is pressed and with a suggested reordering, (2) topologically sorts moves whose destinations are currently occupied by an ally who is also moving — the vacate-then-fill case, which is most of a march — and (3) executes them, aborting cleanly at the first failure with everything before it committed and everything after it untouched, and saying exactly where it stopped. Cheaper partial version if that is too much: let fe7_reachable take a list of slots and return one merged grid annotated with which unit reaches which tile, so I can plan a whole turn from one call instead of one call per unit that goes stale immediately.
